To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) uptake and elimination rates of metals in soil are affected by soil properties; 2) essential and non- essential metals are regulated differently; 3) toxicokinetics can provide valuable information on bioavailability.

(1) Uptake and excretion rates of metals in soil organisms are affected by the properties of both the soil and the organism; (2) Uptake rates of essential metals are not influenced by soil properties but rather controlled by physiological regulation mechanisms; (3) For essential metals, uptake rate constants can be used to assess bioavailability; (4) Uptake rate constants of non-essential trace metals are affected by soil properties and can be used to evaluate bioavailability of these

metal toxicokinetics of soil invertebrates is a function of both metal properties (essentiality, chemical form and solubility) and organism properties (size and feeding strategy) and that metal toxicokinetic parameters can be used for bioavailability assessment of metals in soil.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following topics: (1) uptake and elimination rate constants for different soil invertebrates, (2) the influence of soil properties on the uptake rate constants, (3) the influence of physiological properties on the uptake and elimination rate constant, (4) the influence of exposure concentrations on the uptake and the elimination rate constants.
the uptake and elimination of metals in soil animals, with the aim to understand the mechanisms and to develop models that can be applied for the assessment of metal bioavailability.
the development of new methods for assessing bioavailability and ecotoxicity of metals in soils.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the bioavailability of a certain metal is a function of both the organism and its environment.
the bioavailability of metals to soil invertebrates is a function of the metal, the soil, and the invertebrates, but that it is not a function of the soil-invertebrate interaction.
toxicokinetics in general is a useful tool to assess bioavailability.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
toxicokinetics of metals is a valuable tool to assess bioavailability.
the uptake of non-essential soil-borne metals in invertebrates is mainly controlled by soil properties.
metal bioavailability in soils can be estimated by measuring metal uptake and elimination rates in soil invertebrate species.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of toxicokinetics to assess bioavailability is dependent on metal and organism specific characteristics.
the use of toxicokinetics to assess bioavailability should be done with caution and that the use of a single parameter to describe bioavailability of a specific metal is not sufficient.
the use of toxicokinetics to predict metal bioavailability requires the use of a model that is appropriate to the metal and the organism under study.
